subtitle: People say, he claims, and six more little words
words.intro: In a village in the Eifel, there’s a *Dorfplatz*, a bakery and one bench. Everything anybody needs to know is known there before lunch, and most of it is true.
words.more: Auch im Dorf · also in the village

grammar[0].blocks[0].note: Either way, the speaker isn’t vouching for it.
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: Now or then
grammar[0].blocks[2].title: Rumour, not an order
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: In the news, *Der Minister soll zurücktreten* is usually a rumour: he is said to be resigning.
grammar[0].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: The Eifel is a region of old volcanoes, west of Koblenz. It has crater lakes, the *Maare*, and more crime novels than crime: an entire local genre, the *Eifelkrimi*.

grammar[1].blocks[1].title: In the middle, never stressed
grammar[1].blocks[1].note: After the verb and the pronouns. Stress it and it means something else.
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: False friends
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *wohl* is not “well”, *ruhig* is not “quietly” here, *eben* is not “just now”.
grammar[1].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: Northern Germans say *eben* where southerners say *halt*, and both mean: there’s nothing to be done. *Das ist eben so.* It’s the whole of German philosophy, in three words. Hegel needed eight volumes.

canDo[3]: understand what is said in a bakery
document.intro: A real local bulletin from Dornbirn, Austria, from the first day of 1888, in old type. Every village still has one. It’s where the official rumour goes. *Jänner* is Austrian for January, still.
document.fact: Most German villages still have a *Gemeindeblatt* or *Amtsblatt*, which prints the fire brigade’s dates and who’s had a birthday. It’s often the only paper in the house that everybody reads to the end.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each rumour with soll or will.
document.tasks[1].items[1].prompt: Er sagt, er hat es nie gelesen. (I doubt it)
reading.intro: A stranger has moved into the old mill above the village. Maya has come for a weekend with Lena’s aunt, and she goes to buy rolls. In the bakery, at half past seven, she learns everything there is to know about him. He has lived there for two days.
reading.fact: German has a precise tool for gossip: *Er soll reich sein* means people say so. *Er will reich sein* means he himself claims so, and I doubt it. The same two helper verbs that give orders and wishes here keep you out of a libel suit. Newspapers depend on them.
